full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam J: As common questions of facts and law are involved in these two appeals they were heard together and are being disposed of by this judgment which will govern both the appeals.

2. Appeal No. 234 of 2004 is from judgment and decree dated 18-4-2004 passed in Title Suit No. 100 of 1997 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Gazipur.

3. Similarly, Appeal No. 235 of 2004 arose out of Title Suit No. 101 of 1997 of the aforesaid Court and both the suits were heard analogously by the Court below and by common judgment dated 18-4-2004 both suits were disposed of by the impugned judgment. The trial Court by the impugned judgment decreed both the suits and allowed the prayer for pre-emption made by the plaintiffs in respect of 'A' Schedule property of the respective suits as Shafi-i-Jar under the Muslim Law and being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment the defendant has preferred these appeals before this Court.

4. The crux of the plaintiffs' case is that they are the owner by purchase of the 'B' Schedule land and 'A' Schedule land has been transferred by the vendor i.e. defendant Nos. 2 and 3, to defendant No. 1 on 9-3-1997 and immediately after their knowledge about the transfer of the 'A' Schedule land to the defendant No. 1 they have performed Talab-i-Muwsibat and thereafter, taking certified copy on 18-3-1997 of the sale deeds the plaintiffs definitely came to know that the 'A' Schedule land has been sold to the defendant No. 1 by the other defendants and made Talab-i-Ishhad immediately on 19-3-1997. He performed Talab-i-Ishhad in presence of two witnesses to invoke his right of pre-emption under the Muslim Law.

5. The plaint case, in short, is that the plaintiffs have title to and possession in the 'B' Schedule property by purchase and plaintiffs No. 1 and 2 have title to and possession in 2.58 acres of land i.e. the 'B' Schedule land, which are contiguous to the suit land i.e. 'A' Schedule land in the southern side. The further case is that the plaintiffs have seen construction of wall in 'A' Schedule land in the later part of 1995 by the defendant No. 2 Company as owner. The positive case of the plaintiffs is that on 9-3-1997 the plaintiff No. 2 along with 2 other persons, namely, Messrs Ershad Hossain and Md Ismail Meah were passing through 'A' Schedule land when plaintiff No. 2 found one Abu Bakar Siddique living in a newly constructed CI sheet but and on his query as to who raised the but and how he was living there Abu Bakar Siddique disclosed that the defendant No. 2 Company had sold the 'A' Schedule property to defendant No. 1 Company and defendant No. 1 had raised the but for him as he is the caretaker of defendant No. 1 and upon hearing this the plaintiff No. 2 for self and on behalf of plaintiff No. 1 at once made Talab-i-Muwsibat and asserted their purported right to pre-empt the said land in presence of the said two persons and thereafter, he sent a man to make a query to the local registration office who obtained certified copy of the kabalas in question on 18-3-1997 when he definitely came to learn about the aforesaid transfer and made Talab-i-Ishhad in presence of witnesses telling that Talab-i-Muwsibat had already been made on 9-3-1997. This time Messrs Ershad Hossain and Aman Ali and some other employees of Plaintiff No. 1's company went upon the land of 'A' Schedule. The purchaser is stranger whereas the plaintiffs are neighbors and, as such, they have instituted the suit under the Muslim Law to pre-empt the 'A' Schedule land after due compliance with the formalities as are required under the Muslim Law.

6. Both the suits were contested by defendant No. 1 company purchaser by filing written statement. It is stated that the suits are malafide, fraudulent, misconceived and are not maintainable in their present form according to law and the 'A' Schedule land is not liable to be pre-empted under the Muslim Law as the suit land is neither houses nor gardens. A ground of limitation is also taken in the written statement and it is specifically asserted that Talab-i-Muwsibat and Talab-i-Ishhad has not been properly performed in accordance with Muslim Law and the plaintiffs have no locus standi to file and maintain the suits as Shafi-i-Jar inasmuch as the 'A' Sche-dule land is neither mansion house nor gardens nor small piece of land. All the mate-rial allegations made in the plaint have been denied. The positive case is that the lands alleged to have been purchased by the plaintiffs are well demarcated by boundary wall and the lands of 'A' Schedule are sepa-rated by another pucca boundary wall and boundary wall of 'A' Schedule land is 7.50 ft in height. It is further averred that both the lands of 'A' and 'B' Schedules have boundary walls on all sides having only one entrance gate on the eastern boundary wall by the side of the public road known as Kashimpur Road. It is further asserted that neither on 9-3-1997 nor on any other date the plaintiff No. 2 with Messrs Ershad Hossain and/or Md Ismail Meah passed through or could pass through the 'A' Schedule land as it is surrounded on all sides by a boundary wall and has a gate on the eastern side which leads to Kashimpur Road and therefore, it was not possible for the plaintiff No. 1 or anybody else to enter into or pass through the 'A' Schedule land except through the main entrance gate on the northern side of the eastern wall and the gate remains closed under the supervision of security guard and nobody can enter the 'A' Schedule land without permission and assistance of the employees and security guards of the defendant No. 1. The further positive case of defendant No. 1 is that Abu Bakar Siddique was not present in the 'A' Schedule land on 9-3-1997 as he was on leave

for one month from 25-2-1997. The plaintiffs and their men were aware of all the developments from the time of negotiation between defendant No. 2 and defendant No. 1 for sale and execution of the agreement, cons-truction of CI sheet but and semi-pucca toilets for employees, execution of tripartite agreement and registration of the sale deeds on 7-3-1996 and Messrs YK Ltd installed and fixed signboard on the eastern wall and installed electric and telephone connection in the 'A' Schedule land on their purchase on 7-3-1996. It is also asserted that the lands allegedly purchased by the plaintiffs are bounded on all sides by pucca boundary wall and the plaintiffs are carrying on their manufacturing works therein conveniently and without any inconvenience or difficulty. It further appears that the other side of the story of defendant No. 1 is that the 'A' Schedule land was purchased by defendant No. 2 from different owners with a view to set up an industry thereon and took loan by mortgaging the said land to the Sonali Bank and on their failure to repay the amount, the bank instituted a case in Artha Rin Adalat being Mortgage Suit No. 139 of 1990 and as defendant No. 2 had no other means to liquidate the liability of the bank entered into an agreement for sale with the defendant No. 1 to sell 8.43 acres of land inclu-ding the 'A' Schedule land and subsequently, a tripartite agreement was executed between the defendant No. 1, defendant No. 2 and Sonali Bank and ultimately the entire land was transferred to the defendant No. 1 through different sale deeds pursuant to the agreement and/or these things were within the know-ledge of the plaintiffs. It is also the case of the defendant No. 1 that after purchase of 'A' Schedule land defendant No. 1 sold 0.42 acres of land out of north-eastern part of 'A' Sche-dule land to one Md Serajul Islam through registered kabala dated 16-9-1996 and delive-red specific possession to the purchaser and thus they are in possession of 5.08 acres out of total 'A' Schedule lands. It is also contended in the written statement that neither 'A' Schedule nor 'B' Schedule land has been specified as required by Order VII, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure and on that count also the suit is liable to be dismissed.

7. Mr Tabarak Hussain, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-appellants in both the appeals, argued extensively and also intensively both on point of law as well as facts. Mr Hussain at the very outset raised a question of law as to the maintainability of the suits under Muslim Law inasmuch as the defendant No. 1 is a company incorporated under the Companies Act and it bought 'A' Schedule land from another company i.e. defendant No. 2, of the suit and the plaintiff No. 1 of both the suits is also a company and in the background of these admitted facts he submitted that the instant suits are misconceived and not maintainable for pre-emption under the Muslim Law, inasmuch as a company being a jural person and not being a natural person is not capable of professing any faith. Therefore, neither the appellants nor the plaintiff-respondent No. 1 can be treated as Muslim within the meaning of Muslim Law and the concept of faith as revealed by the Holy Quran can only be followed by a natural person on his own volition. Mr Hussain further submits that a company exists independently of its share-holder and it is now well settled that share-holders of a company are not the owners of a company and they are simply beneficiary of a company. To fortify his submission on this point, Mr Hussain relying on the case reported in ILR 1 (Allahabad) 564 submitted that the settled proposition of law is that a suit filed under the Muslim Law for pre-emption is guided by the law of the vendor and in a case where both the pre-emptor and the vendor are Muslims and the vendee is a non-Muslim in that case also the Muslim Law is to be applied. Therefore, the suit, so far it relates to plaintiff No. 1, is misconceived and not maintainable in law. To fortify his submission he has also relied on the decision reported in 1983 CLC 1983 wherein it has been held that personal law of vendor governs the transaction and not that of vendee for the purpose of determining the right of pre-emption. Mr Tabarak Hussain then also raised another interesting question of law i.e. as to the constitutionality of the law of pre-emption under the Muslim Law. Mr Hussain submits that after the emergence of Bangladesh and coming into force of the Constitution of Bangladesh, certain fundamental rights are conferred upon all the persons irrespective of religious faith and caste or creed, etc. Article 42 of the Constitution ensures right to the property i.e. every citizen shall have the right to acquire, hold, transfer or otherwise dispose of property. Mr. Hussain, to elaborate his submission further submits that the provision of pre-emption under the Muslim Law imposes restriction upon a citizen in the matter of acquisition of property which is, therefore, hit by the provision of Article 42 of the Constitution, inasmuch as the unfettered right of a person either to transfer property or to acquire property is restricted to some extent by the law of pre-emption under the Muslim Law and therefore, it offends Article 42 of the Constitution. To fortify his submission he has relied on the decision reported in AIR 1962 (SC) 1476 wherein the Indian Supreme Court in determining the question of constitutionality of pre-emption law held that restriction imposed by that law in the matter of transfer and/or acquisition of property on the ground of contiguity of land is hit by Article 19(1)(f) of the Indian Constitution. Mr Hussain has also relied on the decision reported in AIR 1980 Allahabad. That was also a case under the Muslim Law wherein the Allahabad High Court took the view that the Muslim Law as to pre-emption in exercise of right as Shafi-i-Jar is void as it imposes an unreasonable restriction on a person in either transferring a property or in acquiring a property from fellow person. In this connection, he has further submitted that Bangladesh is a People's Republic having a secular Constitution although the vast majority of the population professes the faith of Islam and, in that view of the matter, if the Muslim Law of pre-emption is examined in the context of Article 7(2) read with Articles 26, 28 and Article 42 it would lead to the conclusion that the provision of Suffa is not only volatile of Article 42 of the Constitution but is also discriminatory, inasmuch as it confers an additional benefit to a Muslim and on that ground as well the law is liable to be declared void.

8. Mr Tabarak Hussain thereafter made his submission on the merits of the appeal. His first submission is that even if it is found by this court that Muslim Law of pre-emption is a valid law then also the instant suits are not maintainable under the Muslim Law because the plaintiffs are not entitled to get the relief as prayed for, inasmuch as on two. grounds the plaintiffs have instituted the suits, namely, as Shafi-i-Khalid and Shafi-i-Jar and from the impugned judgment it is found that the trial Court found that the plaintiffs were not entitled to get an order of pre-emption as Shafi-i-Khalid and decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff-respondents as Shafi-i-Jar and the plaintiffs have not preferred any cross-appeal against that finding of the trial Court. Mr Hussain now submits that the suit land cannot be the subject matter of pre-emption under the Muslim Law and the plaintiffs cannot invoke the law as Shafi-i-jar, inasmuch as the subject matter is not 'Agar' or land nor the suit land is 'Ruba' or mansion or 'hait' or garden i.e. he contends that a person can invoke the Muslim Law of pre-emption as a Shafi-i-Jar only in respect of a homestead or mansion, garden or small piece of land and in the instant case admittedly, the 'A' Schedule land is not a homestead nor it is garden adjoining to any homestead nor it is a small piece of land, inasmuch as the plaintiffs have instituted the suits for pre-empting 8.69 acres of land. In this connection, he relied on Digest of Muslim Law by Bailee, Tybee’s Muslim Law, section 539 and 12 DLR 93. Mr Tabarak Hussain then submits that it is apparent from the materials and evidence on record that the suit lands have been purchased by the appellant company in order to set up industry and before that the vendor company also bought the land with an intention to set up industry and therefore, the Muslim Law of pre-emption has no manner of application to commercial plots and in decreeing the suit the trial Court lost sight of this important question of law that right of pre-emption cannot be enforced in case of commercial plots. For this proposition, Mr Hussain relies on the case reported in PLD 1990 (Karachi) 387. Mr Hussain made another plank of attack on the impugned judgment by submitting that in decreeing the suits, the trial Court has also committed another illegality in not giving any finding as to the necessity of the suit land by the plaintiffs. In elaborating his submission the learned Advocate further submits that the case of the plaintiffs is that they require the lands for their own purpose but what is the purpose has neither been explained in the plaint nor in the evidence. They simply made a vague statement that the land is required for them. To fortify his submission he contends that one of the stringent principles of law of pre-emption under the Muslim Law is that one cannot resort to pre-emption for his enrichment at the cost of the buyer. Therefore, the plaintiffs were under the legal obligation to explain the necessity of acquiring the 'A' Schedule land by them. But they have miserably failed to discharge their onus on that point. In support of this contention the learned Advocate relied on the decision reported in PLD 1991 (Lahore) 217. Mr Tabarak Hussain then submits, with much emphasis, that the plaintiffs filed the suits for pre-emption as contiguous land owners and thus, they are to prove their ownership of the contiguous land and also required to prove that the legal formalities for the purpose of the Talabs, namely Talab-i-Muwsibat and Talab-i-Ishhad, have been performed at the earliest opportune moment but the plaintiffs have failed to show or establish their ownership or 'Milk' to the 'B' Schedule land by producing cogent evidence both oral and documentary and until and unless the plaintiffs can establish their ownership to the 'B' Schedule land, the plaintiffs will have no locus standi to maintain the suit. In the instant case, the plaintiffs have examined 3 witnesses including plaintiff No. 2 in support of their case but surprisingly, the plaintiffs, for reasons best known to them, did not examine any impartial witness and thus have miserably failed to prove that they are the owners of the 'B' Schedule land and to establish the ownership no document of title has been produced or admitted into evidence by the plaintiffs before the trial Court to establish their title to 'B' Schedule land and it was incumbent upon the plaintiffs to prove their ownership to the 'B' Schedule land in view of the fact that it has been specifically stated by the defendants in their written statement that the plaintiffs are not the owner of contiguous 'B' Schedule land. Mr Tabarak Hussain further submits that the settled proposition of law is that only the owners of the contiguous land can maintain a suit for pre-emption under the Muslim Law as Shafi-i-jar but, in the instant suits, the plaintiffs miserably failed to prove their title to the contiguous land and, in that view of the matter, mere possession of the 'B' Schedule land will not give them any ladder to pre-empt the land. In support of his contention, he relies on the decisions reported in 12 DLR 93 and 1983 CLC 1883.

9. Mr Tabarak Hussain then comes up with another formidable submission and referring to the evidence on record, he submitted that the plaintiff No. 2 in his evidence stated that he does not know what are the requirements of Shafi-i-jar or Shafi-i-Khalid and what formalities are required to perform Talab-i-Muwsibat or Talab-i-Ishhad and this frank and open admission of the plaintiff No. 2 has demolished the entire case of the plaintiffs, inasmuch as a person who does not know what formalities are required to perform for valid performance of Talabs, it is impossible on his part to perform the same. This piece of evidence belies the story of performance of the said Talabs by the plaintiff’s No. 2. In elaborating his submission Mr Hussain submitted that the plaintiff No. 2 as PW 1 said that he performed Talab-i-Muwsibat by saying that he would have bought the 'A' Schedule land and he will exercise right of pre-emption but none of the PWs namely, PWs 2 and 3, supported him in their deposition. Therefore, the plaintiffs failed to prove the performance of the Talabs made by him as claimed in his evidence. Mr Tabarak Hussain further contends that to get a decree for pre-emption under the Muslim Law there must be stringent compliance with the formalities and performance of the formalities must be clearly proved which is absent in the present suits. Mr Tabarak Hussain further submits that the evidence of the PWs shows that the PW 1 did not utter any word to exercise the right of pre-emption whereas law requires that the pre-emptor must express his intention of exercising the right of pre-emption in some way. To further strengthen his submission Mr Tabarak Hussain submits that there is nothing at all on record to show that the formalities of Talabs were performed by the plaintiff No. 1 Company. In this connection, he relies on the decision reported in 49 CWN 761. Mr Tabarak Hussain to fortify his submission submits that the plaintiff No. 1 claimed in the plaint that he performed Talab-i-Muwsibat in the suit land but in evidence he stated that he performed the same standing on the land near the suit lands. Thus, the testimony of PW 1 itself established that Talab-i-Muwsibat was not performed in the suit land. Mr Tabarak Hussain drawing our attention to the evidence of PWs 2 and 3 submitted that they do not support the plaintiffs on this point about the Talab-i-Muwsibat and failure on the part of the plaintiffs to prove the Talab-i-Muwsibat disentitled the plaintiffs to get any relief in the suits. Mr Hussain then submits that the trial Court on misreading and non-consideration of material portion of evidence erroneously held that Talab-i-Muwsibat was properly performed by the plaintiffs for the suit land and thereby the instant appeals are liable to be allowed in the light of the principle of law as laid down in 10 ILR Calcutta 383. Mr Hussain further submitted that the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside yet on another ground i.e. legal pro-position of law is that under the Muslim Law the pre-emptor is required to make Talab-i-Ishhad with the least delay but in the instant case according to the plaint, they came to know about the sale of the suit property on 9-3-1997 and after obtaining certified copy of the sale deeds on 18-3-1997 they made Talab-i-Ishad on 19-3-1997. In this connection he further contends that in making the alleged Talab-i-Ishhad the plaintiffs have failed to comply with the provisions of law because under the Muslim Law pre-emptor is required to make Talab-i-Ishhad either in the presence of the seller or the purchaser or on the subject matter referring to the earlier demand and invoking two witnesses. In this case the admitted position is that the Talab-i-Ishhad was not made either in presence of the seller or the purchaser nor on the suit land. From the evidence on record it appears that the story of making Talab-i-Ishhad by the plaintiff No. 2 on the suit land has not been proved and this aspect of the case was not considered by the trial Court, Mr Hussain contends. In this connection, Mr Tabarak Hussain relies on the decision reported in ILR 17 Calcutta 544, 1991 CLC Karachi 209, 19 DLR 759 and ILR 28 Allahabad 24. Mr Tabarak Hussain referring to the evidence of PW 1 submitted that he himself admitted in his evidence that there is boundary wall on all sides of the suit land and there is only one gate in the eastern side leading to Kashimpur Road and the admitted position is that the plaintiffs' land and the suit lands are demarcated by boundary wall of 7" 6" height all around it. Therefore, there is no contiguity in between the plaintiffs land and the suit land and on that score also the suits were liable to be dismissed. Mr Tabarak Hussain, drawing our attention to the evidences adduced by the PWs, submitted that there are material discrepancies in the evidence of the PWs and on scrutiny it is found that the plaintiffs have failed to prove their case in accordance with the requirement of the Muslim Law. Mr Hussain seriously criticized the finding of the trial Court that the suits are not barred by limitation and in arriving at such a finding the trial Court relied on the evidence of PW 1 who stated that on 9-3-1997 he came to know about the sale of 'A' Schedule land to the defendant No. 1 and then after obtaining certified copy of the sale deeds he made the Talab-i-Ishhad and the instant suits were filed within the period of limitation of one year as contemplated by Article 10 of the Limitation Act. But in affirming at such a finding the trial Court is guilty of non-consideration of the evidence adduced by the DWs coupled with Exhibits A, C and Cl and therefore, erroneously arrived at such a finding and the said finding of the trial Court is contrary to law, inasmuch as it is now well settled within our jurisdiction that under the Muslim Law sale is complete when the vendor on receipt of consideration money inducts the buyer into the possession of land and in the instant case Exhibit 'C' series were presented for registration on 7-3-1996 and from the Exhibit 'C' series it is clear that on receipt of full consideration money the possession of the vendee was confirmed as they were already in possession of the suit property earlier pursuant to the agreement of sale vide Exhibit 'A' and the finding of the trial Court on this point is not sustainable in law, inasmuch as it has been decided by both the Divisions of this Court in the cases reported in 31 DLR 249 and 33 DLR (AD) 359 that in case of pre-emption suit filed under Muslim Law the sale of property shall not be governed by the provisions of section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act and, for that matter, the provisions of sections 60 and 61 of the Registration Act have no manner of application and in order to complete a sale of any property to enable a person to claim pre-emption under Muslim Law, one shall not wait till the completion of all formalities as contemplated under section 61 of the Registration Act and the cause of action arises as soon as the sale is complete under the Muslim Law independent of any written instrument, and here the trial Court fell into an error in holding that the instant suits were not barred by limitation and, in this connection, Mr Hussain has relied on the case reported in 3 DLR 225. Mr Tabarak Hussain then submits that Appeal No. 235 of 2004 arose out of Title Suit No. 101 of 1997 but in the course of evidence PW 1 did not utter a single word in respect of the performance of Talab-i-Muwsibat and Talab-i-Ishhad in respect of the land of this suit. He further submitted that the land of Title Suit No. 100 of 1997 and the title suit No. 101 of 1997 are not one and same and therefore, there is no contiguity of the land of 'B' Schedule with the suit land of suit No. 101 of 1997 and this fact becomes evident from the map of the Advocate Commissioner filed in the suit. It is also contended by Mr Tabarak Hussain that right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage is not available to the plaintiffs, inasmuch as the suit lands are neither houses nor small plot of land and therefore, the suits were misconceived and not tenable in law and in decreeing the suit this aspect of law was overlooked by the trial Court and, as such, the impugned judgments are liable to be set aside.

10. Mr Tabarak Hussain finally submitted that a perusal of the impugned judgment clearly indicates that the trial Court failed to appreciate the legal aspects involved in the suits and also failed to assess the evidence on record properly and the impugned judgment is the product of non-reading and misreading of evidence both oral and documentary and, as such, in any view of the matter the impugned judgment and decree are not sustainable in law.

11. Mr Enayet Hossain Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-respondents in both the appeals, submits that the trial Court taking a correct view of law rightly decreed the suits, inasmuch as the suits are very much maintainable in the present form and manner. In elaborating his submission, he draws our attention to section 231 of the Muslim Law by Mollah and submits that in that section it has been specified what classes of persons can initiate and maintain a suit for pre-emption under the Muslim Law and the expression 'person' includes both natural and jural person. Therefore, the suits instituted by the plaintiffs cannot fail on the ground that the plaintiff No. 1 in both the suits is a company because persons contemplated in that section includes a legal entity and no bar has been imposed on a company under the Muslim Law to file a suit for pre-emption if it fulfils other requirements as laid down in the Muslim Law. The learned Advocate then submits that the trial Court on the basis of the averments of the respective parties framed 3 issues and the appellants are not entitled to make any submission beyond the issues framed by the trial Court and therefore, the appellant must confine themselves in assailing the legality or otherwise of the impugned judgment on the issues that were framed by the trial Court and cannot travel beyond the issues framed by the trial Court for disposal of the instant suits and since the trial Court has found Issue No. 1 in favour of the plaintiffs, it does not lie in the mouth of the appellants to come and say that the suits are not maintainable under the Muslim Law and that the plaintiff No. 1 had no locus standi to institute such a suit. To fortify his argument he relied on the provisions of Order XIV, rule 1 and submitted that a litigant cannot be given the liberty to travel beyond the issues, mores, when the defendants were satisfied with the issues framed by the trial Court. The learned Advocate very empathically submitted that the finding of the trial Court that the suit is not barred by limitation is based on evidence on record, inasmuch as the documents produced by the defendants show that the finding is backed by sufficient materials on record and in elaborating his submission on this point he refers to Clause No. 3 of the agreement dated 16-8-1995 executed by the defendant No. 2 in favour of the defendant No. 1 appellant and it has been clearly stipulated that with the execution of the said agreement the vendee will construct the boundary wall on all sides of the property but the possession will remain with the vendor legally, validly and physically and further that the purchaser shall not claim possession of the property before registration of the sale deed or deeds in favour of the purchaser and relying on the aforesaid clause of Exhibit 'A', submitted that this clearly states the intention of the parties that the title to the property in question will be passed to the buyer when the registration is completed under the Registration Act and the registration was completed on 9-3-1997. Therefore, the trial Court taking a correct view of law rightly held that the suits were instituted within the period of limitation as laid down in Article 10 of the Limitation Act, 1908. He further submitted that in view of the specific stipulation as laid down in Exhibit 'A' mere presentation of the documents for registration on 7-3-1996, did not complete the sale on that date and provision as laid down in Muslim Law will not be applicable in computing the period of limitation. Mr Khan then submits that much emphasis has been given by the appellants that the suit lands are not agricultural land they are commercial lands and thus the suits as framed are misconceived ones and not tenable in law but he submits that it does not reflect the correct state of affairs as contemplated by Muslim Law. Under the Muslim Law a person can initiate a proceeding to exercise the right of pre-emption in respect of an immovable property of any description and it is immaterial whether it is homestead or agricultural or commercial plot and that cannot be a ground for setting aside the impugned judgment.

12. To meet the argument made by Mr Tabarak Hussain on the constitutionality of the law of pre-emption under the Muslim Law Mr Khan in order to repel the same submitted that the provisions of pre-emption as contained in the Muslim Law is not vocative of Article 42 of the Constitution nor it is discriminatory within the meaning of Article 28 of the Constitution inasmuch as Muslim Law is personal law of those who profess the faith of Islam. The plaintiff No. 2 is Muslim and the share-holder, of plaintiff No. 1 are also Muslims and thus the trial Court has rightly applied the provision of Muslim Law in disposing of the instant suit. Mr Khan further submits that neither in the written statement nor in the course of argument before the trial Court this question was agitated by the defendant before the trial Court and after losing in the Court of first instance they fall back on such a subtle and complicated question of law on which the trial Court had no opportunity to express its opinion. Therefore, it would be too late for the defendants to raise the question of constitutionality of Muslim Law of pre-emption and Courts in this Sub-Continent are applying Muslim Law of pre-emption amongst the Muslims even before the partition of India during the British Rule. Mr Khan further submits that the decisions which have been relied on by Mr Hussain should be critically examined by this Court and in the context of our country those two decisions should not be followed in deciding such an important question of law.

13. Mr Khan then turns his attention on the merit of the appeal and submits that the trial Court on consideration of the pleadings, the evidence adduced by the parties and taking into consideration the materials on record rightly found that the plaintiffs have complied with the formalities of Talab-i-Muw-sibat and Talab-i-Ishhad within the meaning of the Muslim Law. in elaborating his argument on this point, he submits that the plaintiff No. 2 has performed those formalities for and on behalf of plaintiff No. 1 and on his behalf though at the time of deposition he stated that he made the Talabs for pre-empting the properties under the Muslim Law and there is no discrepancy in the evidence of PWs. The learned Advocate for the respondent submits that there is no specific form for performing the Talab-i-Muwsibat though certain formalities have been laid down for the performance of Talab-i-Ishhad and from the deposition of PW 1 it becomes clear that the specific intention for pre-empting the suit land by the plaintiffs have been expressed on 9--1997 by performing the Talab-i-Muwsibat on the suit land. Mr Khan further submitted that it does not lie in the mouth of the appellant to say that the plaintiffs have failed to prove their ownership in the 'B' Schedule land, inasmuch as the DWs in one voice admitted in their evidence that to the contiguous south of the suit land, the land of the plaintiffs are situated. Mr Khan submitted that there is sufficient oral evidence adduced by the plaintiffs stating that they are the purchaser of 'B' Schedule land and the certified copies of the deeds in question have been exhibited by the plaintiffs before the trial Court and the original title deeds could not be produced as they are lying with the Bank. In elaborating his submission he further submits that besides the PWs the DWs also admitted that the plaintiffs are the owner of the 'B' Schedule land and the legal position is that things admitted need not be proved. There-fore, even in the absence of any evidence the trial Court is justified in arriving at a finding that the plaintiffs are the real owner of the 'B' Schedule land and thereby the first pre-requisite for filing of the suit for pre-emption by the plaintiffs have been fulfilled. Mr Khan further submitted that Mr Tabarak Hussain forcefully argued that the suit lands are not agricultural land and are commercial plots, but this submission is contrary to material and evidence on record. Exhibits 5(Kha) and 3 (Gha) i.e. Khatian and rent receipt, as well as the title deeds of the defendant No. 1 show that the suit land is agricultural land and the 'B' Schedule land is Chala land and Chala land is also agricultural land within the meaning of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1951. Therefore, it cannot be said that the lands in question are commercial plots and therefore, cannot be a subject matter of pre-emption under the Muslim Law. Mr Khan further submitted that to prove the ownership of the 'B' Schedule land the plaintiffs produced and exhibited current rent receipts which have been admitted without any objection and it is now well settled that khatian and rent receipts are documents of possession and collateral documents of title as has been laid down in 35 DLR (AD) 216. Mr Khan further submitted that it has been contended by the appellants that the plaintiffs did not make the Talab-i-Ishhad promptly but there is no basis for that as admitted facts show that the plaintiffs first came to know about the sale in question on 9-3-1997 and on the next date sent their man to the local Registry Office and obtained the certified copy of the sale deeds on 18-3-1997 when the plaintiffs acquired a definite know-ledge as to the sale of the suit lands by the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 to the defendant No. 1 and then on 19-3-1997 made Talab-i-Ishhad. Mr Enayet Hossain Khan in the course of argument also submitted that in a suit for pre-emption the plaintiffs need not establish their title, inasmuch as the title of the plaintiffs is not in issue and it has been categorically stated by the plaintiffs in their plaint that they are owner by purchase of the 'B' Schedule land which has not been denied by the defendants in their written statement. Therefore, it must be presumed that the defendants have admitted the aforesaid statement of the plaintiffs and now they cannot resale from that and take a different stand giving a go-by to the earlier stand. Mr Khan also submitted that the trial Court has rightly taken the view that the boundary wall erected in between the 'A' and 'B' Schedule lands cannot stand in the way of the plaintiffs to get an order of pre-emption in their favour inasmuch as the 'B' Schedule land is contiguous to 'A' Schedule land.

14. Mr Hossain has intensively and extensively argued about the constitutionality of the law of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage, i.e. the right to pre-empt as a 'Shafi-i-Jar i.e. as owner of adjacent immovable property. It appears that the question of void ness of Shafi-i-Jar has not been agitated before our Court until now though the point has been urged before the Indian jurisdiction in 1962 and the same question also came up for consideration before the Supreme Court of Pakistan. Initially, in the Indian jurisdiction there was difference of opinion at the High Court level as to whether right of pre-emption based on vicinage is constitutional or not and that controversy has been set at rest by the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Bhauram vs Bhijnath AIR 1962 (SC) 1476 and the case of Saint vs Labh Singh reported in AIR 1965 (SC) 314. It has been held by the Indian Supreme Court that a statutory or a cautionary right of pre-emption based on vicinage is unconstitutional as it imposes un-reasonable restriction upon the right to acquire property as guaranteed to a citizen in India under Article 19(1)(f) of the Indian Constitution but the Indian Supreme Court, however, upheld the validity of such a right based on co-ownership and on certain appendages, such as a common stair and a common entrance. As against that the position in Pakistan is that the question of constitutionality of law of pre-emption under Muslim Law came up for consideration in the case of Allah Box vs Jano and others reported in PLD 1962 (WP) Karachi 317. In that case it was argued that the law of pre-emption is in conflict with Article 11 of the late Constitution of Pakistan and, as such, it was not a valid law. The Karachi High Court following the decision of the Pakistan Supreme Court which is reported in PLD 1958 (SC) 533 = 11 DLR (SC) 1, i.e. the case of State vs Doss and another, held that the law of pre-emption as applicable to that part of the Province was in operation and therefore, held that it was wrong on the part of the appellant's Counsel to say that the law of pre-emption was no longer in force. Their Lordships of the Karachi High Court negative the contention that the law of pre-emption comes into conflict with Article 11 of the Constitution on the ground that at that time there was no fundamental right in force under the Marital Law regime as the chapter of fundamental rights in which Article 11 occurs, having, according to their Lordships of the Supreme Court, disappeared from the "new legal order", the argument advanced by the learned Counsel is not available to him and on that count the law of pre-emption was upheld. It thus appears that in Pakistan the question was raised at a point of time when the citizens had no fundamental rights guaranteed to them as the Constitution was abrogated. But after returning to Constitutional Rule the question does not appear to have been re-agitated. So far Bangladesh is concerned, it appears that the constitutionality of right of pre-emption based on vicinage either under the Muslim Law or under the provisions of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1951 has not been called in question and it is only in this case that Mr Hussain has urged this point for the first time.

15. To effectively deal with the question we shall have to consider the provisions as contained in Part III of our Constitution and particularly the provisions as contained in Articles 27, 28(1), 31 and 42 read with Article 7(2) of the Constitution. Before we enter into the discussion on this point it would be pertinent to keep in mind the background and the legal status of Muslim Law of Pre-emption. It must be borne in mind that the Muslim law of pre-emption is not an Islamic Institution. It emanates partly from Arab culture and partly from custom. The basis of law of Shafi-i-Jar under the Muslim Law is based on the saying of the great Prophet of Islam "neighbor has a right superior to that of a stranger in the land adjacent to him." It is based on the ground of convenience and its object is to prevent possible vexation arising from disagreeable neighbor. Here it also must be remembered that right of pre-emption is not one of the matters in suits respecting which the Muslim law is expressly declared to be applicable when the parties are Muslims within the meaning of section 37 of the Civil Courts Act, 1887 rather, the Courts in British India applied it on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience in between the Muslims in claims for pre-emption except in the province of Madras Presidency where that right of pre-emption was not recognized at all unless by local customs and the Madras High Court refused to recognize the rights of pre-emption as it places a restriction upon the liberty to transfer property which is opposed to "justice, equity and good conscience" and in that case right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage was refused. Here it may also be mentioned that in British India the law of pre-emption in some states was regulated by special Acts, namely in Punjab by the Punjab Pre-emption Act of 1913 which in 1924 had been extended with some modification to the North-West Frontier Province. It is regulated in Oudh by Oudh Act (Act XVIII of 1876) and in Agra by the Agra Pre-emption Act of 1922. In those States, therefore, the Muslim law of pre-emption was not in operation except on the footing of local customs. In British India right of pre-emption was recognized as a custom among the Hindus who were either natives or domiciled in Bihar, Sylhet and certain parts of Gujarat and it was governed by the rules of Muslim law of pre-emption. Thus, in India the Muslim law of pre-emption was applied by the royal courts during the Mughal period among the Muslims and among the non-Muslims as well and that legacy was followed even by the British after they conquered India from the Mughals. Thus Muslim law of pre-emption is found in common use among the Muslims not as their personal law but on the ground of justice, equity and good conscience and among the non-Muslims as customary law during the British rule in this sub-continent.

16. During the British rule in Bengal Muslim Law was applied among the Muslims and for the first time by incorporating section 26F in Bengal Tenancy Act, 1882 the provision for pre-emption was introduced for all citizens irrespective of caste or creed and that concept of pre-emption is borrowed from the Muslim law of Shafi-i-Sharik and Shafi-i-Jar but no such provision was available to the non-Muslims for pre-empting any sale of urban property. It is only after the coming into force of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 the non-Muslims could also exercise their right of pre-emption in respect of town property. Thus, an anomaly existed in undivided Bengal during the British regime. A Muslim could exercise right of pre-emption both in respect of urban and agricultural properties whereas a non-Muslim could only exercise their right of pre-emption in respect of agricultural properties until 1949. There was another discrepancy. The limitation for instituting a suit under section 26F was 3 years whereas limitation for pre-emption under Muslim Law was and is one year as provided by Article 10 of the Limitation Act. Besides, under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or under the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, in order to pre-empt a sale, the pre-emptor has to pay an amount to the extent of 10% or 5% above the consideration as the case may be. Thus, a citizen other than a Muslim is worse off in initiating a pre-emption proceedings under the general law, whereas under the Muslim law no such amount is required to be deposited in the Court.

<u>17. Keeping this background in mind, let us now address the issue raised by Mr Hussain. The question, thus raised in this appeal is, whether a right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage offends Article 42(1) of the Constitution. We have already indicated that the Muslim law of pre-emption came into operation during the Mughal period and it continued throughout the British rule but there was no fundamental right guaranteed to a citizen until after partition in 1956 when the late 1956 Constitution was promulgated. The right to property as guaranteed by Article 19(1) (f) of the Indian Constitution is similar to the right guaranteed to a citizen of Pakistan under Article 11 of the late 1956 Constitution. Then came the present Constitution in 1972 after emergence of Bangladesh wherein Article 42(1) reads as follows :</u>

<u>"Subject to any restrictions imposed by law, every citizen shall have the right to acquire, hold, transfer or otherwise dispose of property and no property shall be compulsorily acquired, nationalized or requisitioned save by authority of law."</u>

<u>Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act reads as follows:</u>

<u>"96 (1). If a portion or share of a holding of a rayed is transferred, one or more co-sharer tenants of the holding may, within four months of the service of the notice given under section 89, or, if no notice has been served under section 89, within four months of the date of the knowledge of the transfer, apply to the Court for the said portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves; and if a holding or a portion or a share of a holding is transferred, the tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred may, within four months of the date of the knowledge of such transfer apply to the Court for the holding or portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves;"</u>

<u>Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act reads as under:</u>

<u>"24(1) If a portion or share of the non-agricultural land held by a non-agricultural tenant is transferred, one or more co-sharer tenants of such lands may, within four months of the service of notice issued under section 23 and, in case no notice has been issued or served, then within four months from the date of knowledge of such transfer, apply to the Court for such portion or share to be transferred to himself or to themselves, as the case may be."</u>

<u>Whereas the law of pre-emption under the Mohammedan Law finds its place in section 231 of Mulla's Principles of Mohammedan Law which runs as follows:</u>

<u>Who may claim pre-emption. The following three classes of persons and no others, are entitled to claim pre-emption, namely:</u>

<u>(1) a co-sharer in the property(w) (shafi-i-sharik):</u>

<u>(2) a participator in immunities and appendages, such as a right of way or a right to discharge water (y) (shafi-i-khalit); and</u>

<u>owners of adjoining immovable property (z) (shafi-i-jar), but not their tenants (a), nor persons in possession of such property without any lawful title (b) (Baillie, 481).</u>

<u>18. A combined reading of the aforesaid sections clearly indicate that so far it relates to agricultural land both the Muslims as well as non-Muslims, i.e. all citizens of Bangladesh, stand at par. In case of a non-Muslim he can invoke his right under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act whereas a Muslim citizen can invoke his right of pre-emption either under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or under the Muslim Law. Only difference is that if he resorts to Muslim law he has a limitation of one year whereas limitation under section 96 is for 120 days from the date of knowledge. So far it relates to non-agricultural land, a Muslim can enforce his right of pre-emption either under the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act or under the Muslim Law whereas a Non-Muslim can only resort to the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Under the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act only a co-sharer in land can initiate a proceeding but under the Muslim Law contiguous land owner can also avail the opportunity. It, therefore, appears that the Muslim Law of pre-emption is applicable to both agricultural and non-agricultural lands and the non-Muslim citizen is likely to be worse off in the case of non-agricultural land as he has a shorter period of limitation and he is also to pay 5% more above the sale price. In Article 28(1) it has been laid down that the State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. It, thus, appears that Muslim Law of pre-emption so far it is applicable to the urban property is discriminatory and a Muslim citizen is placed at a higher plain than the other non-Muslim citizens of the State and this also affects the secular nature of the Republic. We are, therefore, of the opinion that Muslim law of pre-emption so far it relates to the town property is void on the ground that it discriminates between a citizen and a citizen on the ground of religion and faith, inasmuch as under section 24 of the Act a non-Muslim contiguous land holder cannot maintain an action for pre-emption but a Muslim can.</u>

<u>19. So far the Raiyati holding is concerned, a Muslim and a non-Muslim stands at par more or less except that there is no provision to invoke pre-emption under section 96 of the Act as Shafi-i-Khalid. It surprises us that neither during the Pakistani days nor even after the emergence of Bangladesh the constitutionality of pre-emption law on the ground of vicinage has ever been challenged before this Court. Article 42(1) laid down that subject to any restriction imposed by law, every citizen shall have the right to acquire, hold, transfer or otherwise dispose of property. It goes without saying that any restriction imposed by law must be a reasonable restriction otherwise it will negate the right conferred on a citizen by Article 31 of the Constitution and Article 42 must be read with Article 31 of the Constitution. The right conferred by Article 42 must be a meaningful right. We are, therefore, of the opinion that restriction imposed by law within the meaning of Article 42(1) of the Constitution must be a reasonable restriction although the word 'restriction' is not qualified by the word 'reasonable' as otherwise it would be arbitrary.</u>

20. In the light of our aforesaid observation, let us now see if the privilege conferred upon a Muslim citizen to invoke the law of pre-emption, as a Shafi-i-Jar imposes any unreasonable restriction upon a citizen either in the matter of acquiring a property or holding a property and/or in the matter for transfer of property. We have already indicated that Muslim law of pre-emption applies to both town and village property and we have to judge the reasonableness of the law in the context of the fundamental rights which have been conferred upon the citizens by the Constitution on the people of this country and which were not there when the Courts in the Sub-continent have considered the reasonableness of the law. If there were no law of pre-emption a vendor would be entitled to sell his property to anybody at a reasonable price that could be settled between him and the purchaser. This right to transfer property freely is clearly restricted by the law of pre-emption which in many cases results in depression of the price which the vendor could otherwise be able to get for his property. Similarly, it also imposes a restriction on a citizen to acquire a property. Suppose, if a property is bought by a landless people and the contiguous land-holder as a Shafi-i-Jar pre-empts the sale and substitutes himself for the purchaser, in such a situation the purchaser is in a helpless situation. He has money to buy property but he cannot acquire it because of the sword of Shafi-i-Jar which hangs over his shoulder. It also adversely affects the vendor in that he cannot get the proper price from a prospective buyer as the prospective buyer will be always under the threat of losing his newly acquired property through an action of pre-emption. It, therefore, appears to us that the privilege available to a Muslim citizen as a Shafi-i-Jar adversely affects the interest of both the vendor and the vendee and in a country where there is explosion of population and tremendous pressure on land the attempt to keep the land in the hands of the contiguous land holder cannot be justified. Moreover, this right of contiguous land owner also offends the rule against perpetuity as the lands are not allowed to change hands freely. As a result the possibility of development of land and improvement of quality in the life of the community suffers. In the context of present- day reality and the globalization of the world the restriction imposed on transfer of property and/or acquiring property by the law of pre-emption, such as Shafi-i-Jar, cannot be encouraged as such a restriction impedes national interest.

<u>21. We have already indicated that Muslim Law of Pre-emption is not a Quranic law. It is adopted by the Courts on the ground of "justice, equity and good conscience". But from our discussion made above, it is clear that it is not only discriminatory and volatile of Article 42(1) of the Constitution but is also opposed to the principle of justice, equity and good conscience and therefore, the Suffa as Shafi-i-Jar is void.</u>

<u>22. Thus, we hold that the law of pre-emption as laid down in section 231(3) in Mullah's Principles of Mohammedan Law, i.e. right to pre-empt a sale as a Shafi-i-Jar which is right of pre-emption based on vicinage, appears to be unconstitutional and offends the provision of Article 42(1) read with Article 31 of the Constitution as it imposes an unreasonable restriction on power of alienation of property and/or acquiring property. So, the provisions of Muslim law of pre-emption, so far it relates to Shafi-i-Jar, is declared to be void as it offends Article 42(1) of the Constitution.</u>

<u>23. Now it requires us to advert to the question of maintainability of the suits under the Muslim Law. The admitted position is that in the instant case both the vendor and one of the vendees are companies incorporated under the Companies Act. A company is, no doubt, a rural person having its own entity and can sue or be sued in its own name but it is not a natural person like a normal human being. Moreover, a company exists independently of its shareholders and shareholders are not the owner of the company. A company being a juridical person is incapable of professing any faith. The admitted position is that Muslim Law is the personal law of the Musalmans. The legal position is that personal law of vendor governs a transaction of sale of immovable property and not that of vendee for the purpose of determining the right of Suffa i.e. pre-emption. A company being an artificial person cannot have any faith in any religion and therefore when the vendor of an immovable property is a company the Muslim Law cannot have any manner of application to that transaction. Two legal propositions have been laid down by the Full Bench of the Allahabad High Court in the case reported in ILR 1 ALL. (FB) 564. The first one is that even if one of the preemptors is Muslim nevertheless the pre-emption will be governed by the personal law of the vendor and the second one is that where the vendor is a Hindu a suit to enforce the right of pre-emption founded on Muslim Law is not sustainable. In the instant case, vendor is a company so also is one of the vendees i.e. plaintiff No. 1 is a company and they are incapable of having any faith in any religion. Therefore, in the facts and circumstances of the case there is no scope to invoke the provisions of Suffa under the Muslim Law. The suits are misconceived and not maintainable in their present forms and manner. In this connection it may be mentioned that Mr Khan half heartedly urged before us that in section 231 of Muslim Law it is stated that three classes of persons are entitled to claim pre-emption and since a company is a legal person it can maintain a suit for pre-emption under the Muslim law. This submission is absolutely devoid of any substance. What is Muslim law? It is the personal law of a Musalman and who is a Musalman? A natural person who professes the Islamic Faith, that is, acknowledges that there is but one Allah and that Mohammad (SM) is his Prophet. A person can be Musalman either by birth or by conversion. Thus only a natural person can become a Musalman and profess the faith of Islam. A juridical person is incapable of following any religion. The courts today apply Muslim Law to the Musalmans only and this power is derived from and regulated partly by Statutes of Imperial Parliament read with Article 152 of the Constitution of Bangladesh and also by our own legislation and the rules of Muslim Law of pre-emption are applied to Muslims as a matter of justice, equity and good conscience. It must also be remembered that right of pre-emption is not a purely Islamic Institution. It emanates partly from Arab Customs and partly from local customs. It was created in a Shafi (pre-emptor) by Hadis of Holy Prophet (SM).Thus we find force and substance in this submission of Mr Hussain and hold that the suits as framed are not maintainable under the Muslim Law. It is true plaintiff No. 2 is a natural person but the suits as framed cannot be maintained by him solely as there is no averments in the plaint nor in evidence to show contiguity of his land with the suit land.</u>

<u>24. A drowning man catches at a straw. So is the case with Mr Khan. Having found himself at the end of a blind alley, in a desperate attempt to come out of it Mr Khan submitted that no such plea was taken by the appellants in their written statements nor any issue was framed to that effect. Therefore, it is too late for them at the end of the day to agitate this issue before this Court. It is true no specific issue was framed to that effect but it appears that in paragraph No. 8 of the written statement it was pleaded that the plaintiffs have no locus stand to file and maintain the suits and the privilege of Muslim Law of pre-emption is not available to the plaintiffs. Besides, it is a question of law which can be agitated at any stage of the suit in the interest of justice, equity and good conscience. Moreover, it is the duty of the Court to decide the legal issue no matter whether it is agitated by the parties or not. On top of that ultimately, Mr Khan also conceded that issue No. 1 as framed, in fact, covers the point. In view of our aforesaid discussion we are of the opinion that the trial Court while dealing with issue No. 1 overlooked this most important question of law and thus erroneously held that the suit is maintainable in its present form and manner. The aforesaid finding is absolutely illegal and contrary to law and not sustainable in law. We, therefore, reverse the said finding and hold that the plaintiffs cannot invoke the right of Suffa in the facts and circumstances of the case.</u>

25. These appeals were heard at length and both the parties argued extensively both on point of law and facts. Therefore, we would also like to address all the issues that were raised by the parties. The trial Court found the suits not barred by limitation whereas it is contended by the appellants that the suits are barred by limitation. Mr Khan relying on clause 3 of the agreement, Exhibit 'A' submitted that it is clearly laid down in that clause that title of the vendor will remain with them until and unless the sale deed is registered and the sale deeds were entered in the volume on 5-3-1997 and Talab-i-Muwsibat was made on 9-3-1997 and after obtaining certified copy on 18-3-1997, Talab-i-Ishhad was made on the following day. Therefore, the suits as filed on 30-3-1997 are well within the period of limitation. As against that, Mr. Hussain's contention is that under the Muslim Law sale becomes complete on delivery of possession of immovable property on receipt of consideration. The sale deeds were presented for registration on 7-3-1996. Thus, if the sale in question is governed by the rules of Muslim Law sale was completed on 7-3-1996 as it appears from Exhibit 'C' series that both the deeds were presented for registration on 7-3-1996 and possession of the suit land was also handed over to the defendant-appellant long before the execution and presentation of the sale deeds for registration pursuant to agreement for sale vide Exhibit 'A'.

26. Now we are to see if section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act superseded the provisions of Muslim Law. In India initially there was divergence of opinion but that controversy has been set at rest by the Indian Supreme Court by holding that section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act superseded the provisions of Muslim Law. Their view is that sale of immovable property by a Muslim does not become complete on delivery of possession of the property on receipt of consideration and execution of the instrument of sale until and unless it is entered into the volume of the registration office i.e. until and unless the provisions of sections 60 and 61 of the Registration Act is complied with. But our Appellate Division in the case reported in 33 DLR (AD) 359 took a different view. It has been held that section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act did not supersede the Muslim Law and that for a valid sale under the Muslim Law, requirements are offer by the vendor; acceptance by the vendee, passing of the consideration as settled in the contract and delivery of possession. After negotiation is complete and the moment the vendor accepts the consideration and puts the vendee into possession sale is complete.

27. The Privy Council in the case reported in AIR 1923 PC 41 = 48 IA 475 held that in determining what system of law will apply to a sale is to be ascertained from the intention of the parties. Earlier in (1900) 35 Cal 575, the question was as to whether there had been a sale for the purpose of determining the application by applying the principle of Muslim Law of pre-emption. It was held that the real solution was to be found by determining, in each case, what was the intention of the parties. These two cases, amongst others, were considered by the Appellate Division in 33 DLR case and on a review of all the leading decisions of the superior Courts of this Sub-continent, ultimately held that right of pre-emption under Muslim Law is not dependent on registration of the deed of sale and one claiming pre-emption under the Muslim Law must make necessary demand on the completion of sale of the property as contemplated under the Muslim Law and when under Muslim Law sale is completed we have already stated.

<u>28. There is another aspect of law. Both the Calcutta High Court and the Privy Council is of the view that what law will govern depends on the intention of the parties. But fact remains that in a pre-emption suit the pre-emptor is not a party to the agreement for sale. It is between the vendor and the vendee. So, when the pre-emptor in a given case intends to invoke the provision of Muslim Law to exercise his right of Suffa under the Muslim Law he must make the necessary demands when the sale is complete under the Muslim Law and need not wait for completion of the sale under the general law, if he does, his right of suffa may be defeated by various devices. The instant suit is under the Muslim Law. No doubt, in the agreement it is stipulated that the sale shall not be completed unless the sale deed is registered. But this stipulation cannot stand in the way of the pre-emptor if he wants to pre-empt the sale under the Muslim Law. In the present case the plaintiff has instituted the suit under the Muslim Law but it appears that he made the demands long after the sale was completed under the Muslim Law. The admitted position is that the agreement Exhibit A was executed on 16-8-1995 and part payment was also made on that day and physical possession of the property was also handed over to the vendee. On receipt of payment of full consideration the sale deed was executed and presented for registration on 7-3-1996 and the suit was filed on 30-6-1997 which is well beyond the period of limitation. It thus appears that the suits are also barred by limitation but unfortunately, this material legal aspect of the case was totally lost sight of by the trial Court and in arriving at a finding that the suit is not barred by limitation it erroneously relied on the provisions of General Law which has no manner of application to the instant case. The view taken by us gets support from the decision reported in 33 DLR (AD) 359.</u>

<u>29. Let us, now, discuss about the merits of the appeals. The defendants have denied the ownership of the plaintiffs in the "B" Schedule land in paragraph No. 12 of the written statement as well as DW 1 has denied it in his evidence. As against that the plaintiffs made out a case in their plaint that they are the owners by purchase of the "B" Schedule land but at the time of adducing evidence except the word of PW 1 there is no other documentary evidence to show that they are the real owners of the "B" Schedule land. It is stated by PW 1 that the original title deeds are lying with the bank and a letter to that effect of the Bank was produced but they have not admitted in evidence the certified copy of the title deeds. Mr Tabarak Hussain empathically argued on this point submitting that it is pre-requisite for the plaintiffs to prove their ownership in the contiguous land. Even before this Court the plaintiff respondent did not file any application under Order XL, rule 31 of the Code to admit those documents as additional evidence. Moreover, there is no explanation why they have not exhibited the title deeds which are the most important documents for proving the title of the plaintiffs to 'B' Schedule land. To counter the arguments of Mr Hussain, Mr Khan appearing for the plaintiff-respondent tried to impress upon us that though title deeds have not been exhibited nevertheless khatians and rent receipts which are collateral documents of title have been produced and exhibited. Mr Khan relying on the decision reported in 35 DLR (AD) 216 submitted that record of rights and rent receipts are collateral documents of title and these are sufficient to establish the title of the plaintiff. As against that, Mr Hussain has submitted that in a pre-emption suit it is the sine qua non to establish the ownership of the plaintiff and by withholding the original documents without giving any explanation and production of Khatian and rent receipts are not sufficient to establish the title and in support of his contention he has relied on the decision reported in 12 DLR 93. In this connection it may further be mentioned that though they have produced some certified copies of the deeds but that only relates to 2.58 acres of land and regarding the rest of the land no title deed has been filed and ignoring this material aspect of the case, the trial Court arrived at a finding that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their owner-ship simply on the ground that even the DWs have admitted plaintiffs' ownership. This observation of the trial Court appears to be based on misreading of the evidence of DWs. It appears that DW 1 categorically denied the ownership of the plaintiffs and the other DWs admitted that the plaintiffs are in possession of the 'B' Schedule land. But they did not indicate the nature of possession as to whether they possess it as owners or otherwise. It is now well established that in a pre-emption suit the plaintiff must establish his exclusive ownership into the contiguous land as Shafi-i-Jar. Therefore, finding of the trial Court that the plaintiffs are the owners of the 'B' Schedule land is erroneous and against weight of evidence.</u>

30. There is no dispute between the parties that in order to succeed in a pre-emption suit, it is the legal requirements that the plaintiffs must prove Talab-i-Muwsibat followed by Talab-i-Ishhad. In the plaint, it appears that the plaintiffs' case is that Talabs were made by the plaintiff No. 2 on behalf of himself and on behalf of the plaintiff No. 1 company, but while giving evidence he has shifted from that stand and stated that he made the Talab on his own behalf. Therefore, from the testimony of PW1 himself, it appears that the case of making Talabs by the plaintiff No. 1 falls to the ground. Now, there is controversy between the parties as to whether the alleged Talabs were performed in accordance with law. In the plaint the averment is that when the plaintiff No. 2 along with Messrs Arshad Hossain & Md Ismail Mia were passing through the land of Schedule 'A' he found Abu Bakar Siddique living in the newly constructed CI sheet but and on plaintiff No. 2's query as to who had raised the but and how he was living there, he disclosed that the defendant No. 2 company had sold the Schedule 'A' property to the defendant No. 1 company for a consideration of Taka 31,90,000 and defendant No. 1 had raised the but for him as his caretaker and upon hearing this, the plaintiff No. 2 (for self and on behalf of the plaintiff No. 1) at once by way of immediate demand (Talab-i-Muwsibat) asserted their right to pre-empt the said land by demanding in the presence and within the hearing of the said Mr Abu Bakar Siddique to buy the property in Schedule 'A' from the defendant No. 1. But in evidence plaintiff No. 2 as PW 1 stated that “আমি ৯-৩-১৯৯৭ ইং তারিখে এ তফসিলের সম্পত্তির কাছ দিয়া যাইতেছিলাম। আমার সাথে ছিল এরশাদ ইঞ্জিনিয়ার, ইসমাইল হোসেন আরো কয়েকজন। আমি তখন এ তফসিলের জমিতে একটি টিনের ছাপড়া ঘর দেখতে পেলাম। ঘরের সামনে একজন লোক দেখলাম। তাহার নাম আবু বকর। আমি তাহাকে জিজ্ঞাসা করিলাম আপনি এখানে কিভাবে আসলেন এবং ঘরটি কে করল। তখন আবু বকর সিদ্দিক বলিল ঘরটি ইউনুস কোঃ ইউ, কে টেকসটেইলে করিয়াছে এবং এই জমিটি খরিদ করিয়াছে ও আমাকে কেয়ার টেকার রাখিয়াছে। আমি তখনই আবু বকরকে বললাম এই সম্পত্তি আমি খরিদ করিতাম। আমি জানলে খরিদ করিতাম। তখন আমি বলি আমি এই সম্পত্তি প্রিয়েমশন করিব কথাটি আমার সাথের লোকজন সকলেই শুনিয়াছে।PW 2 also stated “নালিশী জমি চিনি। ৯-৩-১৯৯৭ ইং তারিখ এ বিকাল ৪ টার দিকে নুরুল ইসলাম বাবুল, ইসমাইল ও আমি হাটিয়া যাইতেছিলাম।তখন পাশের জমিতে দেখি যে, একটি ছাপড়া। তখন চেয়ারম্যান নুরুল ইসলাম বলে যে, এই ঘরে কে আছে তখন একটি দাড়িয়ালা লোক বাহির হইয়া আসিয়া বলে যে, আমি মালিক ইউনুস সাহেবের কেয়ার টেকার। হাজী ইউনুছ এই জমি কিনছে তা্ই সে উহা দেখাশুনা করে। তখন চেয়ারম্যান বলে এই জমি তো আমি কিনবো। আপনার মালিককে টাকা ফেরত নিতে বলবেন”। PW 3 stated in his deposition that “গত ইং ৯-৩-১৯৯৭ তারিখ এ বিকাল ৪ টার দিকে যমুনার চেয়ারম্যান আসে তখন আমি তাদের দেখিয়া সেখানে যাই। চেয়ারম্যান আমাকে সাথে করে নালিশী জমিতে যাইয়া একটি জমিতে যাইয়া একটি সাইনবোর্ড ছাপড়া দেখি এবং আমাকে বলেছে যে সাইন বোর্ড টা কে দিয়েছে দেখ। আমি ঐ ঘরে যে ছিল তাকে দিলে একটি লোক বাহির হয়ে আসে। তার নাম আবু বকর। তাকে জিজ্ঞাসা করায় বলেছে, আমার মালিক ইউনুছ কোঃ কে সম্পত্তিটা কিনছে। তখন চেয়ারম্যান বলেছে, তোমার মালিক জায়গাটা কেন কিনলো এই জায়গা আমার বাউন্ডারীর লাগা জমি। ইহা আমার খুবই দরকার তাই মালিককে বলো যেন টাকাটা আমি দিয়ে দিব আর জমিটা আমাকে দিয়ে দেয়।”

31. So far Talab-i-Muwsibat is concerned these are the evidences adduced by the plain-tiffs. From the evidence of PWs 1 and 2 it appears that Talab-i-Muwsibat was made by PW 1 when they were passing by the side of 'A' Schedule land but the evidence of PW 3 contradicts them on this point as PW 3 said that PW 1 went to 'A' Schedule land accompanied by him. That PW 3 has made a false statement in this regard is established from other admitted facts. It is admitted that 'A' Schedule land is surrounded by a brick wall of about 7 feet high and it has only one gate on the eastern side of the land facing Kashimpur Road. So, the story of going to the 'A' Schedule land does not inspire confidence, mores when PWs 1 and 2 in one voice said that they were walking by the side of 'A' Schedule land. That PW 3 on this score made a false statement is also proved by his own statement made in cross-examination when he stated “যমুনা নিটিং টা চারদিকে বাউন্ডারী ওয়াল দিয়া ঘেরা যাহার উচ্চতা অনুমান ৬-৬.৫০ ছয় বা সাড়ে ছয় ফুট। বিবাদীর জমিটা বাউন্ডারী ওয়াল দ্বারা বেষ্টিত। বিবাদীর ২ টা গেট। একটি বড় ও একটি ছোট পার্শ্বে গেইট পূর্ব দিকে দিয়ে করা। বিবাদীর ২ গেইটের মধ্য দিয়ে কোনদিন ঢুকি নাই।”

32. Thus the story of entering into the suit land by the plaintiff No. 1 or by the other PWs is demolished. It further appears that neither of the PWs 2 and 3 has ever stated that PW 1 performed Talab-i-Muwsibat and also asserted that he will also perform Talab-i-Ishhad.

33. The legal position is that Talab-i-Muw-sibat has to be followed by Talab-i-Ishhad. Law requires that in order to perform Talab-i-Ishhad witnesses have to be invoked. But in the instant case neither PW 2 nor PW 3 uttered a single word that PW 1 took them along with him to be a witness for the performance of Talab-i-Ishhad. Further, there is no evidence that while performing Talab-i-Ishhad PW 1 has never stated that he has also earlier performed Talab-i-Muwsibat. The law is that one need not enter into the suit land for making Talab-i-Muwsibat, but the legal requirement is that if the Talab-i-Muwsibat is not made on the suit land then Talab-i-Ishhad must be made either in presence of the buyer or in presence of seller or on the land transferred. In the instant case it is not the case of the plaintiffs that they had made Talab-i-Ishhad either in presence of the buyer or the seller. In that case it becomes the bounden duty of the plaintiffs to make Talab-i-Ishhad on the suit land. We have already noted the discrepancy and incongruity in the evidence of all the PWs that the plaintiff No. 2 never entered into the suit land is proved both by oral as well as documentary evidence. In the plaint it is averred that there is a pathway across the 'A' Schedule land and this averment is falsified by the evidence of PW 1 himself. PW 1 admitted that 'B' Schedule land is surrounded by a boundary wall all around it having an height of 6.5 feet. It is also in evidence that 'A' Schedule land is also surrounded on all sides by another boundary wall. Besides, the admitted position is that to the east of 'A' and 'B' Schedule lands there is a road which runs from north to south and that is a motorable road. It is also in evidence that trucks ply through that road to enter the 'B' Schedule land where plaintiffs have two industrial undertaking. Thus it is improbable and unlikely that a leading industrialist of the country like PW 1 will walk down to his industrial unit on foot regularly, moreso in high sun through a motorable road. The boundary wall of 'B' Schedule land is 7.6 feet high and thus it is also unbelievable that one could see the tin shed in 'A' Schedule land from the road. Further, it appears that on both the occasions PW 1 was accompanied by 5/6 persons but out of them he produced and examined two persons as PWs 2 and 3 who are partisan and could not produce a neutral person as witness. The case made out by the plaintiffs appears to be that everybody was appearing just when it would be necessary under the law for him to appear and everybody was behaving just as it was necessary for him to behave if the plaintiffs were smoothly to exercise the right. This aspect of the case was not considered by the trial Court. On examination of the evidence of PWs 2 and 3, it appears that PW 1 has not been corroborated by these two witnesses in the matter of Talab-i-Ishhad. PW 1 stated that when he made Talab-i-Ishhad he also stated that earlier he made Talab-i-Muwsibat but neither of them corroborated PW 1 on this point. Another legal requirement is that the Talabs must be made at the earliest opportunity without wasting any time. In the instant case, the plaintiffs have failed to comply with this requirement as well. The settled position of law is that under the Muslim Law sale is complete when the offer made by the vendor is accepted by the vendee followed by the passing of the consideration from the vendee to the vendor and delivery of possession is given to the vendee. Thus the moment the vendor accepts the consideration and puts the vendee into possession sale is complete and it gives rise to the right of pre-emption. In the instant case, possession was handed over on 16-8-1995 when the deed of agreement was executed and the full consideration was paid on 9-3-1996 when the deed of sale was executed and presented for registration under the Registration Act. Therefore, sale was completed on 9-3-1996 whereas Talab-i-Muwsibat was made on 9-3-1997 long after the completion of the sale. This aspect of the law was also overlooked by the trial Court.

34. Now let us examine the legal position in this regard. In the case reported in ILR 10 Calcutta 386 it has been held that in order to sustain a claim for pre-emption it is essential that the ceremony of Talab-i-Muwsibat must be properly performed. In ILR 17 Cal 544, it has been held by the Full Bench of the Calcutta High Court that when a person claiming a right of pre-emption has performed the Talab-i-Muwsibat in the presence of witnesses, but not in the presence either of the seller or of the purchaser, or on the premises, it is necessary that when performing the Talab-i-Ishhad he should declare that he has made the Talab-i-Muwsibat and at the same time should invoke witnesses to attest it. Similarly, in the case reported in ILR 28 Allahabad it was held that the mere fact that the Talab-i-Ishhad is made in the presence of certain persons at the place where it is made is not sufficient to make the demand a good one unless those persons are specifically called upon to bear witness to the demand being made. In 49 CWN 761 it has been held that the right of pre-emption as is stated in the Hedaya, is an exceedingly feeble right, it gives one the power of diseasing another who has acquired a property in a bona fide manner for good value, and if it is to be exercised, the ritual of the Talabs must be observed to the letter. The right is strictissimijuris and the slightest deviation from the formalities required by law will prevent its accrual. The same view is re-iterated in 19 DLR 759. In that decision it has been held that after having made Talab-i-Muwsibat the pre-emptor has to affirm his intention with the least practicable delay referring expressly to the fact that Talab-i-Muwsibat had been made. It requires the pre-emptor to make an express reference to Talab-i-Muwsibat. Thus omission at the time of making the Talab-i-Ishhad about Talab-i-Muwsibat is indeed, fatal to the claim of pre-emption. If the pre-emptor in making the second demand failed to call the attention of the witnesses to the fact that he had already made the first demand the second demand is not valid.

35. On an analysis of the aforesaid decisions, it appears that it is essential for claiming the right of pre-emption under Muslim Law that there must he clear proof of the observance of all the formalities. The essential requirements of Talab-i-Ishhad appear to be:
