(a) that the Talab should be made against the seller, if the property sold is still in his possession, or against the purchaser, or upon the property sold:

(b) That the Talab should be made in the presence of not less than two witnesses:

(c) That while making Talab-i-Ishhad, reference is required to be made about the Talab-i-Muwsibat.

<u>36. Thus, in order to invoke the provisions of Muslim Law while claiming pre-emption the formalities prescribed by law must be strictly complied with and the doubt, if any, in respect of Talabs is to be resolved in favour of the vendee. We have already quoted the relevant portion of the deposition of PW 1 and it is clear from the evidence that while making Talab-i-Ishhad he did not make any reference to Talab-i-Muwsibat. There is also no evidence that PW 1 invoked PWs 2 and 3 to witness the Talab-i-Ishhad. It further appears that the Talabs were never made either to the vendor or the vendee. It is, however, asserted by PW 1 that he made the Talab-i-Ishhad on the 'A' Schedule land but we have already found this part of the evidence of PW 1 unbelievable. Moreover, PW 1 in cross stated that “দেঃ ১০১/৯৭ নং মোকদ্দমার এ তফসিল জমি এবং দেঃ ১০১/৯৭ নং মোকদ্দমার এ তফসিল ভুমি এক কিনা বলিতে পারিব না।”Admittedly, the aforesaid suits were heard analogously. But the pre-emptor failed to point out on which portion of the 'A' Schedule land the alleged demands were made. This is also fatal for the pre-emptor. PW 1 further stated in cross that তালাবী মছিবত ও তালাবী ইশাদ কাহাকে বলে তাহা আমি বলিতে পারিব না। If that be so how he could perform the Talab in accordance with the provisions of Muslim Law. Besides, PW 2 and PW 3 are silent about the reference of Talab-i-Muwsibat while making Talab-i-Ishhad. The consistent view of all the superior courts of the sub-continent is that at the time of making demand non-reference to the first demand is fatal to the case of the claimant of the right of pre-emption. For the foregoing reasons we are constrained to hold that the plaintiffs-respondents have miserably failed to prove the performance of the Talabs in the instant case which is fatal for the plaintiffs. These are very much important legal issues but in holding that the plaintiffs have been able to prove the making of Talab-i-Muwsibat and Talab-i-Ishhad, the trial Court not only ignored these legal aspects of the case but is also found to be guilty of misreading and/or misappreciating the evidence on record and the finding of the trial Court on this point is not borne out by the evidence and materials on record.</u>

<u>37. In this connection it may further be mentioned that admittedly plaintiff No. 1 is a company and plaintiff No. 2 is the Managing Director of that company. If a company wants to pre-empt a land as contiguous land owner, it is incumbent upon the company to show that they are authorised to exercise that right by the Memorandum of Association of the company. A company cannot do a thing unless it is authorised to do so i.e. unless that power has been given to the company by the Memorandum of Association. The Memorandum of Association has not been produced before the Court nor any Board resolution has been produced to show that the company has ever decided to buy the suit land. Besides, there is also no resolution showing that the plaintiff No. 2 has been authorised to file the case on behalf of the company as well. The plaintiff No. 1 is not a natural person and it acts through its Board of Directors. If the company wants to buy any land it must so decide in a Board meeting. No resolution of such Board meeting has been produced. It is also not averred in the plaint that the Board in its meeting decided to buy the suit land. These are the requirements of law. There is no averment in the plaint nor there is any evidence adduced that the plaintiff No. 1 had ever decided to go for pre-empting the suit land as contiguous land holder. Besides, it is neither averred nor proved by any oral or documentary evidence that PW 1 as Managing Director of plaintiff No. 1 was authorised to exercise such authority on behalf of the company. Withholding of the Memorandum of Association and the non-production of any Board resolution showing that the plaintiff No. 1 company has decided to file the instant suit speaks volumes against the plaintiffs. Thus, the suit so far it relates to plaintiff No. 1 is also not maintainable on this count. In this connection it may also be mentioned that with- holding the impartial witness who admittedly accompanied. PW 1 on 9-3-1997 and 19-3-1997 also speaks volumes against the plaintiffs and it appears to us to be a fit case where adverse presumption can be drawn that if any of the neutral persons would have been examined they would not support the case of the plaintiffs.</u>

<u>38. It further appears to us that in decreeing the suits the trial Court failed to appreciate the scope and purpose of the law of pre-emption under the Muslim Law. The plaintiffs have instituted the suit as Shafi-i-Jar, but admittedly, the suit land is a vast tract of land consisting of about 6 acres. The defendant-appellant has purchased the suit land to set up industries and so is the intention of the plaintiff-respondents. Though the suit land is recorded as agricultural land but the admitted position is that in the vicinity of the suit land industrial units are established. Even the plaintiffs have set up two industrial under-takings on the 'B' Schedule land. Thus by now the land has been changed to industrial land. It is also evident from Exhibit 'A' that the land was bought by the vendor to set up industry and, as such, it is assessed as industrial land. The object behind the application of the law of pre-emption is to safeguard the privacy of Muslim families. Right of pre-emption, therefore, cannot be enforced in case of commercial lands because the question of disagreeable neighbor in such cases does not arise. The view taken by us gets support from the case reported in PLD 1990 Karachi 387.</u>

39. There is another aspect of the case. The plaintiffs are owner of 2.58 acres of land whereas they have instituted the instant suit to pre-empt 8.69 acres of land as Shafi-i-Jar. The legal position is that a claim to right of pre-emption on the ground of vicinage alone will not lie in the case of large estates and is available only when either houses or small holdings of land are transferred. Pre-emption under Muslim Law is to prevent the inconvenience which may result from the introduction of a disagreeable stranger as a coparcener or as a near neighbour. Its object is to prevent possible vexation arising from a disagreeable neighbour.

40. Baillie's, Mohammedan Law certainly seem to us to favour the contention that pre-emption on the score of vicinage was only intended to apply to houses or to small plots of land which for obvious purposes, if put up to sale, it might be convenient for the neighbour to purchase. Thus the settled principle is that some claims on mere vicinage are good when either houses or small holdings of land are transferred. But this principle does not apply to large estates. From this point of view also the suit is not maintainable and is ill-conceived.

<u>41. In decreeing the suit the trial Court failed to consider yet another important question of law. The right of pre-emption is a clog on the right of a citizen to deal with his property freely and such curtailing of owner's right to deal with his property must be construed very strictly. Under the Muslim Law the right of pre-emption is allowed to a claimant in consideration of his necessity and not as a matter of luxury. This principle should always be kept in mind while determining the claim of pre-emption. The plaintiffs are already owners of vast tract of lands i.e. the 'B' Schedule land. They have already erected two industries in two different portions of the 'B' Schedule land and unutilized lands are still there. The plaintiffs have never explained why they need the suit land. We have already indicated that the suit land is not 'Agar' or houses or small land. "Agar" or land alone can be the subject matter of pre-emption where the subject matter of pre-emption consists of a share in a village or a large estate. But neither a neighbor who is not a co-sharer nor a participator in appendages can claim it on the ground of merely of vicinage. See ILR 33 All 28. Thus there is another hurdle and a formidable one for the plaintiffs-respondents to cross. Under Muslim Law, right of pre-emption/Suffa cannot be made the vehicle for enrichment but is to be exercised under extreme necessity.</u>

<u>42. Further, the Suit No. 101/04 appears to suffer from legal defect inasmuch as it is in pleading and in evidence that part of the 'A' Schedule land i.e. 0.42 acres of land, has been sold to one Md Serajul Islam by defendant No. 1 but that land has also been included in the 'A' Schedule which cannot be pre-empted, inasmuch as that land was sold on 16-9-1996 by registered Kabala No. 14020. There is no pleading that in respect of that 42 decimals of land any talabs were made nor there is any evidence on record to that effect. Besides, the plaintiffs have failed to demarcate and identify the lands of Suit No. 101 of 2004 and also failed to establish the contiguity of land with 'B' Schedule land. On top of that, the plaintiffs have failed to comply with the provisions of Order VII, rule 3 of the Code.</u>

43. Before we part with these appeals, we need to advert to the other appeal that is Appeal No. 235 of 2004. We have already noted that two suits were filed by the plaintiffs in respect of two different sale deeds and they were registered as Title Suit No. 100 of 2004 and 101 of 2004 respectively and both the suits were heard analogously by taking one set of evidence and by a common judgment both the suits were decreed. From the impugned judgment it appears that the trial Court disposed of both the suits on the basis of issues framed in Title Suit No. 100 of 1997. From the record of Title Suit No. 101 of 1997, it appears that in that suit two more issues were framed. But at the time of writing out the judgment, the trial Court was confined to issues framed in Title Suit No. 100 of 1997 and did not at all care to give any finding about the other two issues framed in the later suit. In disposing Title Suit No. 101 of 1997 the trial Court did not deal with the said issues which demonstrate that the trial Court most negligently and without applying its mind to the facts and circumstances of the case in a mechanical way decreed the suit without properly addressing the relevant issues.

44. It has already been indicated that both the appeals are being disposed of by this Judgment and at the time of advancing argument Mr Khan however did not advance any argument in respect of Title Suit No. 101 of 1997 that is Appeal No. 235 of 2004. It is admitted that the land of Appeal No. 235 of 2004 and the land of Appeal No. 234 of 2004 were purchased by two different kabalas, but the plaintiffs did not adduce any evidence whatsoever in respect of Talabs for the land of Title Suit No. 101 of 1997 and this is a material omission and failure on the part of the plaintiff-respondents to prove that they had also exercised their right of pre-emption in respect of the land of Title Suit No. 101 of 1997 and that they had performed the Talabs, the plaintiffs cannot get any relief in Appeal No. 235 of 1994 on this score alone. Mr Hussain urged this point emphatically for the second appeal, but in our opinion it is of no importance, inasmuch as we have already found on merits that the appeals are liable to be allowed as the trial Court judgment suffers from patent illegality and infirmity and is not sustainable in law. Thus, no doubt, the omission on the part of the plaintiffs to adduce evidence in respect of the suit land of Title Suit No. 101 of 1997 is fatal and this is an additional ground but our finding given on all other points are common to both the appeals, therefore, in any view of the matter, the appeals are liable to be allowed.

45. In the result, both the appeals are allowed judgment and decree dated 184-2004 (decree signed on 18-8-2004) passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Gazipur in Title Suit No. 100 of 1997 and Title Suit No. 101 of 1997 are set aside and both the suits are dismissed. The defendant-appellant No. 1 will get cost in both the suits against the plaintiffs.
